chunks.section: ORCA: The Annealed Spectral Conditioning Optimizer for Faster, Better LLM Training
chunks.text: Yuanshi Liu Boyuan Jiang Liang Hou Xin Tao Pengfei Wan Zhouchen Lin Cong Fang † † thanks: This work was conducted during the author’s internship at Kling Team. Affiliation: School of Intelligence Science and Technology, Peking University Affiliation: Kling Team

Modern LLM optimizers such as Muon often produce weight matrices with higher effective rank than Adam, yet further spectral control has delivered only modest gains. We identify a tension behind this result: concentrated spectra can suppress gradient directions in coupled weight matrices and slow optimization, while constraints maintained throughout training can limit task-specific adaptation and raise the attainable loss floor. We introduce ORCA (Orthogonal Regularization, Cooled After), a minimal optimizer intervention that applies strong but temporary soft orthogonality regularization early in training, then removes it. This allows the weights to benefit from a broader spectrum early on and adapt freely afterward. Across LLaMA, Qwen3, and fine-grained mixture-of-experts models ranging from 130M to 8B parameters, ORCA achieves lower final validation loss than Muon. Its loss reduction relative to Muon matches or exceeds Muon’s reduction relative to Adam. Ablations support the early-shaping, later-release design. Further, ORCA requires no architectural changes and adds minimal overhead. An implementation is available at https://github.com/uuurraaa/ORCA_Optimizer .

Recent matrix-based optimizers such as Muon have shown substantial improvements over Adam in LLM training ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Jordan et al., 2024 ) . A striking difference emerges in their weight trajectories: compared with Adam, Muon maintains a markedly flatter singular-value spectrum and a substantially higher effective rank over most of training, where effective rank is measured as ‖ 𝐖 ‖ F 2 / ‖ 𝐖 ‖ 2 2 \|\mathbf{W}\|^{2}_{F}/\|\mathbf{W}\|^{2}_{2} . The two optimizers start from comparable values, but Adam exhibits a much sharper decline early in training and remains consistently below Muon thereafter. This observation suggests a natural hypothesis: better preserving the effective dimensionality of weight matrices may be an important ingredient behind faster optimization. This emerging importance of spectral structure has motivated an important and growing line of work that explicitly preserves or promotes favorable spectral structure during training ( Qiu et al., 2026a ; Shi et al., 2026 ; Dong and Sawin, 2026 ) . These approaches introduce principled mechanisms for controlling the weight spectrum and have demonstrated promising improvements in LLM optimization. If a higher effective rank is indeed beneficial, however, one might expect stronger spectral control to yield correspondingly larger gains. In practice, the improvements over Muon are often more modest than this intuition would suggest, despite substantially stronger control over the weight spectrum.

To understand this gap, we examine two competing effects of spectral control that arise simultaneously. We begin with a matrix factorization model ( Gunasekar et al., 2017 ) that abstracts the multiplicative coupling common in Transformer architectures. On the benefit side, we illustrate that a well-shaped spectrum allows more gradient directions to contribute to other parameter updates, facilitating faster optimization. On the cost side, however, imposing spectral constraints limits model expressiveness and can raise the attainable loss floor. Correspondingly, controlled interventions during Llama training empirically support both effects. Together, these results point to a seemingly trade-off between faster optimization and model expressiveness.

However, we argue that this trade-off is not fundamental. Spectral regularization may be most valuable early, when it can shape the optimization trajectory, yet become a liability if maintained as the weights adapt to the task. The two effects need not be accepted together: we can use the constraint to shape the spectrum, then release it before it restricts the final solution. This motivates a minimal method ORCA (Orthogonal Regularization, Cooled After): During an initial phase, ORCA applies a soft orthogonality penalty, R orth ​ ( 𝐖 ) = 1 4 ​ ‖ 𝐖𝐖 ⊤ − 𝐈 ‖ F 2 R_{\mathrm{orth}}(\mathbf{W})=\frac{1}{4}\|\mathbf{W}\mathbf{W}^{\top}-\mathbf{I}\|_{F}^{2} . Then directly removes it at a single switch point. Training thereafter follows the standard optimizer update, with no gradual decay or further changes. This design lets early regularization influence the optimization path without prescribing the spectrum throughout training. In our experiments, this simple release is followed by faster loss reduction and a lower final validation loss than Muon. Figure 1.1: LLaMA 130M training dynamics. Effective rank is measured on a middle-layer V V projection; the dashed line marks regularization release. Figure 1.1 illustrates the transition. While the penalty is active, the effective rank of the weight matrix rises sharply above Muon’s, although ORCA initially has a higher validation loss. After release, the rank falls from its peak but remains above Muon’s, while validation loss decreases rapidly, crosses the Muon curve. The result is consistent with early spectral shaping leaving a useful effect on the subsequent trajectory, even after the explicit penalty is gone. Controlled interventions in Section 5 further investigates into this connection.

We evaluate ORCA on LLaMA, Qwen3, and fine-grained MoE models ranging from 130M to 8B parameters, including 100B-token training runs. ORCA achieves lower final validation loss than Muon across these settings. In most experiments, the reduction is 0.02–0.04, comparable to or greater than Muon’s gain over Adam. To put this loss reduction in perspective, on LLaMA 1.3B, ORCA achieving the 0.024 lower validation loss reaches Muon’s 100k-step loss in just 60k steps. Further, downstream evaluations, alternative early spectral interventions, multi-seed runs, and ablations of method parameters and intervention timing further support these gains. Together, these results show that early spectral shaping followed by constraint relaxation can improve training efficiency and final performance across architectures without substantial changes to the optimizer. To summarize the contributions of the paper: (1) We illustrate a trade-off in spectral control through a simplified model and empirical observations: favorable spectra can accelerate optimization but persistent constraints may harm the attainable solution quality. (2) We introduce ORCA, a minimal shape-then-release optimizer that leverages early orthogonal regularization to improve optimization trajectories while allowing unconstrained adaptation in later training. (3) We demonstrate ORCA’s effectiveness across diverse LLM architectures and scales, achieving faster convergence and lower loss than existing optimizers. Through extensive controlled experiments, we further validate the mechanism that early effective-rank shaping drives the observed improvements.

The high effective rank naturally maintained by Muon can support optimization without prescribing a fixed spectral geometry for the final weights. By contrast, increasingly restrictive spectral constraints preserve the desired structure by reducing the freedom of the model to adapt its spectrum as training proceeds. The appropriate goal is therefore not to maximize effective rank at every point in training, but to retain enough spectral support to avoid path-side bottlenecks while still allowing the spectrum to adapt to the task.

The preceding analysis reveals a tension between the trajectory-side benefit and the endpoint-side cost of spectral control. Broad spectral support can facilitate optimization along the training trajectory, while enforcing the same structure persistently may restrict task-adaptive solutions at the endpoint. This suggests a temporal design principle: spectral control should shape the early optimization trajectory, but be released before it restricts task adaptation. ORCA (Orthogonal Regularization, Cooled After) is a minimal two-stage realization of this shape-then-release principle. During an initial active stage, ORCA applies spectral shaping to steer the early trajectory away from spectrally concentrated regimes. After this stage, the shaping term is removed completely and training reverts to standard Muon. This separation allows spectral control to influence the optimization path without prescribing the spectral geometry of the final solution.

The hard switch is the simplest implementation of the shape-then-release principle. The early intervention is used to steer the optimization trajectory away from spectrally concentrated regimes, rather than to prescribe a persistent spectral constraint. Once released, the spectrum is free to adapt to the task objective. Empirically, we find that part of the higher-effective-rank state induced during the active stage persists after release, allowing the optimization benefit to continue without maintaining the orthogonal regularizer. Unless otherwise specified, we use τ = 0.25 \tau=0.25 throughout the paper; Section 5 studies sensitivity to the release point. Beyond soft orthogonality. Soft orthogonality defines the default ORCA optimizer, but the underlying shape-then-release principle is not tied to this particular spectral operator. In Section 5, we replace soft orthogonal shaping with alternative early spectral interventions, including Pion-start and DiagSVD variants. These methods differ in how the spectral state is shaped during the active stage; once the active window ends, the intervention is removed and all variants continue with the same released Muon dynamics. This provides a controlled way to study whether the benefit of early spectral intervention extends beyond soft orthogonality itself.

Implementation and overhead. In the standard setting, ORCA adds two matrix multiplications per weight matrix during shaping without changing the communication complexity; the remaining operations are fused into the optimizer update. Our Muon baseline performs 24 matrix multiplications across eight Newton–Schulz iterations, so shaping increases the multiplication count by 2 / 24 = 8.3 % 2/24=8.3\% . This extra work disappears after release. We batch matrices of identical shapes to reduce kernel launches, use dedicated kernels, and form the Gram matrix along the shorter dimension. On the 8B MoE model, average distributed optimizer update time is 227.2 ​ ms 227.2\,\mathrm{ms} for Muon and 237.4 ​ ms 237.4\,\mathrm{ms} for ORCA. The 10.2 ​ ms 10.2\,\mathrm{ms} difference amounts to approximately 0.8 % 0.8\% of a roughly 1.3 ​ s 1.3\,\mathrm{s} training step. Peak memory is 101.41 ​ GB 101.41\,\mathrm{GB} and 101.66 ​ GB 101.66\,\mathrm{GB} , respectively. Overall, ORCA incurs negligible additional training overhead in this configuration.

In this section, we verify the efficacy of ORCA on three specific issues: (1) Llama pretraining with grid learning rate search and larger scale pretraining. (2) Pretraining task on Qwen3 architecture with the additional QK-norm that may violate the matrix factoring reparameterization. This section focuses on the efficacy of ORCA, and for more robustness test of parameters and controlled interventions on gain of ORCA, readers can refer to Section 5 .

Setups. We pre-train Llama-series models Touvron et al. (2023) ranging from 130M to 1.3B parameters on C4 , using 25B to 100B tokens. We also pre-train Qwen3-series models Yang et al. (2025) ranging from 160M to 0.6B parameters on The Pile ( Gao et al., 2020 ) , using 25B to 100B tokens. Finally, we train fine-grained mixture-of-experts models ranging from 0.8B to 8B parameters on OLMo-mix-1124 ( OLMo et al., 2024 ) , the data mixture including DCLM-Baseline ( Li et al., 2024 ) using 25B to 100B tokens. We first run a learning rate grid-search for Adam, Muon, Pion and ORCA. All trials share the same data, batch size, sequence length, and 50k-step training budget. We use 𝐎 t = 0.2 / Rms ⁡ ( 𝐎 t ) ⋅ 𝐎 t \mathbf{O}_{t}=0.2/\mathrm{Rms}(\mathbf{O}_{t})\cdot\mathbf{O}_{t} to rescale the Muon and ORCA update where 𝐎 t \mathbf{O}_{t} is the Newton-Schulz orthogonalization output to align the update with the Adam’s ( Liu et al., 2025 ) . We perform a two-stage coarse-to-fine learning rate grid search. The coarse sweep evaluates { 5 × 10 − 4 , 10 − 3 , 2 × 10 − 3 , 5 × 10 − 3 } \{5\times 10^{-4},10^{-3},2\times 10^{-3},5\times 10^{-3}\} . Once the coarse sweep locates a candidate learning rate, we evaluate the neighbors on its both sides to refine the best lr within a smaller local range. The refinement grid consists of { 6 , 8 } × 10 − 4 \{6,8\}\times 10^{-4} , { 1.3 , 1.6 } × 10 − 3 \{1.3,1.6\}\times 10^{-3} , and { 3 , 4 } × 10 − 3 \{3,4\}\times 10^{-3} , which reduces the local spacing between learning rates candidates to about 1.2 × 1.2\times – 1.5 × 1.5\times . All four optimizers use this protocol and the same tuning budget.

The advantage of ORCA holds over a wide range of learning rates: at every learning rate evaluated for both methods, ORCA reaches a lower final validation loss than Muon, and at all evaluated configurations between 10 − 3 10^{-3} and 5 × 10 − 3 5\times 10^{-3} it is even better than fully tuned Muon. chunks.section: 5 Where the Gain Comes From: Controlled Interventions
chunks.text: Figure 1.1 offers an initial view of ORCA’s mechanism: early shaping raises the effective rank, part of this increase persists after shaping is released, and loss then decreases faster. While Section 4 establishes ORCA’s optimization gains, in this section we vary shaping strength and timing, as well as the form of the early spectral intervention, to isolate their contributions to these gains. Additional controls for optimizer state and learning-rate schedules are reported separately in Appendix C.2 . Retained Effective Rank Predicts Post-Release Gain We first test whether the effective-rank difference retained after release tracks ORCA’s final gain. Holding all other settings fixed, we sweep the shaping strength over γ ∈ { 0 , 0.05 , 0.1 , 0.5 , 1 , 2 } \gamma\in\{0,0.05,0.1,0.5,1,2\} and measure both the average post-release effective rank and the final validation loss. The sweep exhibits a clear dose response. As γ \gamma increases, the retained effective rank rises from about 278 278 to 335 335 , while the final validation loss falls from 2.8466 2.8466 to 2.8106 2.8106 ( Figure 2(b) ). The relation flattens at larger γ \gamma , indicating diminishing returns. This supports retained effective rank as an important variable behind ORCA’s post-release gain.

chunks.text: Release-point sensitivity. We first vary the duration of the initial shaping stage over τ ∈ { 0.10 , 0.25 , 0.40 , 0.55 } \tau\in\{0.10,0.25,0.40,0.55\} on LLaMA 130M. Every setting improves over Muon’s final loss of 2.8512 2.8512 : the four release points reach 2.8210 2.8210 , 2.8106 2.8106 , 2.8107 2.8107 , and 2.8166 2.8166 , respectively ( Figure 2(c) ). The broad effective range shows that ORCA does not rely on a precise release point. We use τ = 0.25 \tau=0.25 by default because it is the shortest tested window in the best-performing range. Together with the effective-rank dynamics in Figure 1.1 , Figure 5.1 shows two effects qualitatively consistent with the simplified analysis: (i) shaping is costly while active. Validation loss rises and remains on a high plateau whenever shaping is imposed, consistent with persistently high effective rank restricting the task-adaptive spectrum. (ii) The benefit emerges after release and requires time. Once shaping is removed, the retained high-rank state supports faster Muon descent without the same endpoint restriction. Early shaping leaves the longest released phase and achieves the lowest final loss. Middle shaping also recovers rapidly and finishes slightly below Muon, but remains worse than early; late, full, and off-then-on shaping leave insufficient or no final released phase and fail to recover by the endpoint. These explain ORCA’s two-stage design: raise effective rank early, then reserve most of training for unconstrained optimization.

ORCA’s mechanistic claim extends beyond soft orthogonal regularization: if raising and retaining effective rank early improves optimization after release, other ways of doing so should yield similar gains. We test this with DiagSVD and Pion-start, comparing them with ORCA and standard Muon in 50k-step LLaMA 130M training. chunks.section: Dependence on the training budget and learning-rate schedule.
chunks.text: ORCA’s benefit requires sufficient training after release. In our experiments, runs with approximately 10,000 10{,}000 optimizer updates or fewer can underperform Muon; we recommend at least 30,000 30{,}000 updates as a practical guideline. Our default shaping window of 25 % 25\% is selected under the WSD schedule and is not necessarily optimal for other learning-rate schedules. In particular, the same active-step fraction S / T S/T can correspond to different fractions of the total learning-rate budget, ρ ⁡ ( S ) = ∑ t = 0 S − 1 η t ∑ t = 0 T − 1 η t , \rho(S)=\frac{\sum_{t=0}^{S-1}\eta_{t}}{\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\eta_{t}}, which provides a useful reference for comparing and adjusting release points across schedules. Nevertheless, Figure 2(c) shows consistent gains over Muon across a broad range of release points, indicating robustness to the release fraction.

chunks.section: Matrix granularity and applicability to router weights.
chunks.text: The granularity at which attention projection matrices are treated is another important implementation choice. Among the configurations we searched, treating 𝐖 Q \mathbf{W}_{Q} and 𝐖 K \mathbf{W}_{K} head-wise while retaining 𝐖 V \mathbf{W}_{V} and 𝐖 O \mathbf{W}_{O} as full matrices performed best. This configuration outperformed both treating all four projections head-wise and treating all four as full matrices. Applying ORCA to router weights also yields benefits in our MoE experiments, suggesting that its applicability extends beyond attention and feed-forward projections.

We emphasize that the main contribution of this paper is the general two-phase optimization principle: introducing a temporary intervention during early training to shape a favorable optimization trajectory, followed by releasing the intervention to restore the flexibility needed for task-specific adaptation. This principle is not tied to any particular optimizer or regularization.

chunks.section: Flexibility in the choice of optimizers.
chunks.text: On the one hand, the framework can be combined with advanced matrix-based optimizers, such as SOAP. On the other hand, it can also be applied to computationally inexpensive optimizers, such as Adam, without introducing sophisticated matrix-based update rules. As demonstrated in our experiments, both SOAP and Adam benefit from the same early-shaping and subsequent-release strategy. This flexibility makes the two-phase framework applicable across different computational budgets and optimization settings.

chunks.section: Flexibility in the choice of regularization.
chunks.text: Similarly, the orthogonal regularizer used in ORCA is only one possible realization of early geometric shaping and can be replaced by either stronger or more lightweight constraints. On the one hand, stronger geometric constraints, such as optimization over a possibly scaled Stiefel manifold, provide more explicit control of the weight geometry and may be particularly beneficial for architectures prone to severe spectral degeneration. On the other hand, lightweight alternatives may offer better scalability. For example, row-oblique constraints enforce equal row norms without requiring orthogonality between rows. Other options include analogous column-wise norm constraints and group-wise orthogonality penalties, which encourage orthogonality only within small groups of rows or columns. These alternatives retain partial control over weight geometry without forming the full Gram matrix, although they generally provide weaker protection against spectral degeneration. When chosen to align with the weight-sharding layout, such constraints can reduce both computation and communication costs relative to full Gram-matrix regularization in large-scale model-parallel training.

ORCA uses temporary early orthogonality regularization to accelerate LLM training, achieving lower validation loss. Its central insight is that optimizers can both choose better update directions and steer early training toward regions where loss is easier to reduce. We hope this perspective inspires future optimizer design.

chunks.section: Appendix A Orthogonal and spectral training.
chunks.text: Kong et al. [2022] developed a momentum optimizer that maintains orthogonality constraints. For LLMs, POET and POET-X preserve weight spectra through orthogonal reparameterization, while Pion preserves them through optimizer updates [ Qiu et al., 2026a , Qiu et al., 2026b , Shi et al., 2026 ] . ISO applies fixed-spectrum optimization to post-training [ Zhu et al., 2026 ] . These methods report impressive training stability and downstream or post-training results; Pion and ISO outperform Muon in several downstream or post-training evaluations. However, persistent spectral constraints have not yet been shown to consistently achieve lower LLM pretraining loss than Muon. Similar attention to weight spectra appears at the model level: the PC layer improves convergence by carefully reparameterizing weights to reshape their spectra [ Wang et al., 2026 ] . Optimizer-side shaping may be more broadly applicable and less costly because it does not modify the model’s forward or backward passes. One key difference in our method is that we remove the orthogonal constraint entirely after early training. We believe this freedom later in training is an important reason for our larger improvement over Muon.

This appendix summarizes the standard pretraining configurations used in the main experiments. We omit the controlled ablations and optimizer-specific interventions discussed in the main text. Unless stated otherwise, all runs use a decoder-only Transformer with RoPE, SwiGLU feed-forward blocks, RMSNorm, and bias-free linear layers. The matrix parameters use Muon or ORCA, while embeddings, the language-model head, and one-dimensional parameters follow the AdamW fallback described in the method section.

We train LLaMA-style models on C4, Qwen3-style models on The Pile, and the fine-grained MoE models on the olmo-mix-1124 mixture [ Gao et al., 2020 , OLMo et al., 2024 ] . The corresponding tokenizers are the T5 SentencePiece Unigram tokenizer (vocabulary size 32,100 32{,}100 ), the Qwen3 tokenizer (vocabulary size 151,936 151{,}936 ), and the OLMo tokenizer (vocabulary size 100,278 100{,}278 ).
